title: Terry Crews on America's growing love for F1
excerpt:
Actor and former NFL player Terry Crews believes Formula 1's growing popularity in the United States is doing more than attracting new fans, with the sport encouraging Americans to embrace different countries and cultures.

Growing up in Flint, Michigan, Crews was surrounded by the automotive industry, with his father working for General Motors. That connection has since come full circle as the star of Brooklyn 99 has made regular appearances at races.

Formula 1's popularity in the United States has continued to grow ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, the country's final race of 2026 season, its American fanbase has grown to 52 million, an 11% increase in 2025.

But Crews believes the sport's growing popularity is having an impact on Americans that extends beyond the racetrack.

"I wouldn't say [Formula 1] is becoming more American. In fact, what I would say is that Americans are becoming more Formula 1.

"The United States tends to be quite insular… When you look at the number one sport in the world, it's football, but if you talk to people in America, they say it's American football. They think the Super Bowl is the biggest sporting event in the world, and actually the World Cup is the biggest.

"Formula 1 has expanded America's minds. When you look at a lot of Americans, they don't even have a passport, because the United States is so big they feel like they're travelling. But because of Formula 1, there's now Americans saying, 'I'm going to Hungary, I'm going to Singapore, I'm going to Monaco.'

"There's so many Americans that I've run into that are like, 'Hey, I watched Drive to Survive, I knew Cadillac was in here. This is my first time out of the United States.'"

Crews is no stranger to international audiences himself, having enjoyed a career spanning television, film and professional sport. And it was F1's global appeal that initially drew him towards the championship.

"One thing that I love is being a worldwide person. It was very important to me, even in my entertainment career, that every project that I do reaches everywhere in the world, and I'll be honest, I'm actually bigger around the world than I am in the US.

"When I go to Brazil, Korea, the UK, or anywhere in the Middle East, it's gigantic, and that's one thing I love. It's a big world, and that's what turned me on about Formula 1 in the first place: the fact that it was a world sport."

Dressing for the occasion

Crews' appreciation for the different cultures on the F1 calendar also extends to his paddock wardrobe. The actor works alongside his friend and business partner, designer Nana Boateng, to create custom outfits for his appearances around the world.

And with races taking place in locations as different as Monaco, Austin and Las Vegas, Crews believes each occasion deserves its own look.

"Most of my [clothing] is custom, simply because my body does not fit off the rack. It took a long time to be able to do things like this, but I'm wearing one of the world's best menswear designers, my best friend and business partner.

"His name is Nana Boateng, and we go through the seasons and pick out what we're doing, how we look. Monaco can't look like Vegas, that can't look like Austin, especially when we're going to Formula 1 races.

"He's tailored my taste. Twenty years ago, I didn't dress like this. It's like hanging out with a wonderful chef. He elevates your taste. McDonald's won't work anymore."

And ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, Crews is ready for even more Americans to take a bite and get the taste for F1.

title: Williams unveil special livery for Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
Williams have unveiled a special livery that will adorn their car for the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend.

The one-off chrome look is a collaboration with the team’s title partner Atlassian, designed to shine under the lights as Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz take to the Las Vegas Strip Circuit. Both drivers will also sport custom race suits and gloves in line with the colour scheme.

In an announcement revealing the livery, Williams stated that the design is “the latest embodiment of Williams and Atlassian’s belief that the fastest way forward is knowing where you have been, which is central to the partnership”.

Team Principal James Vowles commented: “Our next step forward isn’t a matter of reinvention; it’s about evolving from where we’ve been, using the knowledge, context, and information our team shares.

“We’re proud to be working with Atlassian to unlock that near-50-year history and using it as fuel for our future. This spectacular livery reflects that and I’m looking forward to seeing it take to the track under the bright lights of the Vegas Strip.”

Mike Cannon-Brookes, Co-Founder and CEO, Atlassian, added: “The new Williams livery looks great in Las Vegas – but our partnership goes well beyond what you see on the track. We are helping Williams turn their ambition into execution.

“We’re working shoulder to shoulder with the team at Williams to build AI workflows on the Atlassian Teamwork Graph connecting their teams’ expertise, knowledge and projects so they can make smarter, faster decisions.”

title: What time is the 2026 Las Vegas GP and how can I watch it?

title: 5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Las Vegas GP
excerpt:
20 races down, three to go. The 2026 Formula 1 season is set to kick off the final triple-header of the year, and even with the winners of both championships already decided, there are plenty of storylines to get excited about.

Here are just a few of the talking points as the paddock heads to Las Vegas.

Lawson and Lindblad stay

Across the previous triple-header in Austin, Mexico City and Sao Paulo, there was a growing focus on the Racing Bulls driver line-up for 2027.

Arvid Lindblad’s impressive rookie season always looked likely to secure him a second year, as the teenager continues his development and looks to build on multiple point-scoring finishes. However, the other side of the garage appeared to have less certainty over what would happen next.

Liam Lawson has enjoyed an outstanding season, including a very solid three-race run at Red Bull in place of the injured Isack Hadjar at the end of August and early September. The New Zealander has also led the field outside the top four teams on numerous occasions and continued that form even when he didn’t have confirmation of a future seat.

With Racing Bulls weighing up whether to promote the talented Nikola Tsolov into a race seat in 2027, Lawson produced a run of four top seven finishes in five races, finishing ninth behind the two Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull and McLaren drivers in the middle of that stretch in Austin.

Alan Permane’s team confirmed the current pairing of Lawson and Lindblad will continue into 2027 last week, and now the focus will be on the progress Red Bull want to see from each moving forward.

Cadillac’s driver decision

It isn’t just at Racing Bulls where there has been uncertainty over a driver line-up, with Cadillac also considering their options.

Sergio Perez is already committed on a long-term contract, with an extension being announced in Mexico City as a reward for both his strong performances on track but also the work that Perez has been doing to try and push the team forward behind the scenes.

His team mate Valtteri Bottas was also signed for his experience to help develop Cadillac, but there were questions from the team regarding some of his performances during the year, and there was a clear replacement option being explored in the form of Colton Herta.

ANALYSIS: Why the F1 driver market might produce one last twist

The American former IndyCar star received a number of extra FP1 outings in order to help him secure the points required to apply for his FIA Super Licence, and duly reached that target last time out at Interlagos.

That gave Cadillac the ability to weigh up their options over whether they want to stick with Bottas - who is under contract - or give Herta his first opportunity to race in F1.

Ahead of another home race for Cadillac, a decision is understood to have been made, with the expectation that the team will continue with their current experienced pairing into 2027, and an announcement due during the Las Vegas Grand Prix week.

Camara gets another outing

There are so many driver stories to keep an eye on at the moment, and another is more immediate than the two above as Haas adapt to life after Esteban Ocon.

The Frenchman was replaced in the middle of the Mexico City Grand Prix race weekend by Ryo Hirakawa, and the experienced reserve driver duly earned himself a point on debut as he was able to take advantage of post-race penalties for others.

With Hirakawa racing in the World Endurance Championship at Monza the following weekend, Haas then took the opportunity to give their 2027 race driver Rafael Camara an early debut, with the Brazilian taking the seat for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

At the time, Haas made clear the decisions only related to those specific race weekends, and there had been no final call on who would drive for the remainder of the season. Theoretically, Haas could alternate between both Camara and Hirakawa, although they can’t turn to another option without requiring special dispensation from the FIA due to a rule limiting teams to four race drivers per season.

Haas have now confirmed Camara will retain the drive for the rest of the year as they get a head start on 2027, with the 21-year-old building on his first experience during a challenging Interlagos weekend.

Championship battles for drivers and teams

Mercedes wrapped up the Teams’ Championship at the last race in Brazil, one week on from Kimi Antonelli becoming the youngest Drivers’ Champion in history in Mexico. But that doesn’t mean there isn’t still plenty to play for.

From a teams’ perspective, so much of the focus is on who wins the title, but the prize money is paid out based on where each team finishes in the constructors’ standings, meaning each position below P1 still carries a huge amount of weight.

Our writers on Antonelli’s title success and what it means

Ferrari look well placed to wrap up second place overall, but behind that is a close battle for third between Red Bull and McLaren. The double podium at Interlagos allowed Red Bull to pull 17 points clear of McLaren, but it was Lando Norris who took victory in a sign of McLaren’s potential after introducing an upgrade in Brazil.

McLaren Team Principal Andrea Stella says there will be further additions in Las Vegas as they continue developing with 2027 in mind, and they could well help McLaren stay in touch with Red Bull entering the final rounds.

When it comes to the drivers’ standings, it’s more a case of pride being at stake, but Max Verstappen currently occupies second place behind Antonelli after a remarkable run of eight straight podiums - including three victories.

Verstappen is looking to extend his current tally of seven consecutive seasons finishing in the top three in the championship - an eighth would match Lewis Hamilton’s record - but there are just 33 points covering the Dutchman, George Russell, Hamilton, Charles Leclerc and Norris, with all five having won races this year.

A spectacular racing venue

We have seen all sorts of action in Las Vegas since the race joined the calendar in 2023, with last lap overtakes, wet qualifying sessions and reliability issues all playing a role in producing drama at different phases of the weekend.

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit is a unique challenge for multiple reasons, not least the near-two-kilometre-long run along the Strip that sees the cars flashing past a number of the most iconic resorts in the city.

Racing under the lights means competitive track action taking place after dark as temperatures drop, and that means it is often the coldest race weekend of the year as well.

With teams having to juggle energy demands on a circuit with multiple long straights, it could well be another race weekend with plenty of overtaking right up until the final lap.

title: McLaren determined to take fight for P3 ‘down to the wire’
excerpt:
Racing Director Randy Singh is optimistic that McLaren can maximise their performance in the final three rounds and secure third place in the Teams’ Championship, but noted that they don’t “feel any less pressure than the last couple of season finales”.

After clinching back-to-back constructors’ titles in 2024 and 2025, McLaren slipped behind Mercedes and Ferrari in this season’s pecking order, and lost an additional spot to Red Bull during the recent triple header.

However, they received a crucial boost as Lando Norris made the most of their upgrades at Interlagos to take his third victory of the campaign, which could provide the momentum they need to overhaul Red Bull’s 17-point advantage in the standings.

Asked on the latest episode of F1 Nation whether they can close the gap, Singh replied: “We'll do our best to make sure it goes down to the wire and in our favour. We're treating it like a mini championship on our side, so we're just aiming to do our best at each race.

“I think it’s what saw us through both 2024/2025 Abu Dhabi races – there was a lot of pressure. We just try to focus on doing the best that we can in each area, and the result will take care of itself, hopefully.

“It's interesting because it doesn’t feel [like] any less pressure than the last couple of season finales to be honest. We've got three races as well, which is quite nice because we've got plenty of time to try and harvest as many points as we can.

“Everyone's excited and then we get straight into Las Vegas preparation as well. And this week everyone's pretty intense with seeing what we can learn from the last race – both in the dry and in the mixed conditions – and what we can do to prepare for Vegas. So, full activity and steam ahead.”

Since Las Vegas was added to the calendar in 2023, it’s become one of McLaren’s weaker tracks, with costly errors, a lack of pace and even a double disqualification limiting them to a total of just 17 points over three events.

They’re hoping to turn that form around when the paddock heads back to The Strip this week, especially as they have another chance to capitalise on the effective upgrades they introduced in Brazil.

“We all see it as a challenge and a big opportunity for us to really go and get a result at a circuit that we haven't had a good result at yet,” Singh explained. “And so we're all kind of approaching it with that kind of relish.

“We had some good upgrades on the car in Brazil, so we've got some work to do to still keep getting the most out of those. We're really approaching it from that underdog sense of, ‘we've not had a good one there, but we've got a good chance to have a really good result there [this year].

“The upgrades worked well – you can tell that also from Oscar [Piastri], who only had them from FP2 onwards because we missed FP1 in Brazil. Both drivers really quickly got up to speed again, especially Oscar. I think missing an FP1 session is tricky.

“We had the car in a good window in Brazil. We need to try and make sure we do the same in Vegas. It'll be much colder, I think, than it was in Brazil. The grip can be very low. Circuit characteristics are completely different as well.

“So we've got a lot of work to do to try and make sure that we hit the ground running, and that we keep optimising the package as it is now. It's not easy with these cars.

“Whilst we've had these cars now for the best part of a year, the upgrades, as Andrea [Stella] said before, are really quite significant. They changed the way the car behaves and we have to kind of re-learn some of that stuff each time.”

McLaren’s battle for P3 in the Constructors’ Championship was just one of the talking points that emerged in the Las Vegas Grand Prix preview, which saw Jolyon Palmer and James Hinchcliffe join F1 Nation host Tom Clarkson.

title: Haas confirm Camara to race for the team in Las Vegas
excerpt:
Haas have confirmed that Rafael Camara will again race for the team at the Las Vegas Grand Prix – following on from his Formula 1 debut last time out at his home event in Sao Paulo – while Ryo Hirakawa is also set to get behind the wheel during Free Practice 1.

Following Esteban Ocon’s departure during the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, reserve driver Hirakawa stepped in for his maiden race at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez – ending the event with a point thanks to a P10 finish.

Camara – who was announced as one of Haas’ 2027 drivers in October – then made his own debut one week on at Interlagos, with the youngster managing to bring the car home amid challenging weather conditions.

Haas have since announced that the 21-year-old will again get behind the wheel of the VF-26 alongside Ollie Bearman in Las Vegas, offering another opportunity to gain further track time ahead of his maiden full-time campaign next season.

“I’m looking forward to getting back in the car in Las Vegas,” said Camara. “Brazil was a good learning experience, and now the focus is on building on that, improving step by step and making the most of every session.

“It’s a new circuit for me, so there’s a lot to learn, but I’ll do my best to keep progressing throughout the weekend.”

Hirakawa, meanwhile, will make his fourth FP1 appearance of the year for the squad in place of Bearman, two weeks on from the Japanese driver winning the 2026 World Endurance Championship with Toyota Racing.

Haas Team Principal Ayao Komatsu commented: “We're looking forward to kicking off the final triple header of the 2026 season at the famous Las Vegas strip. This street course offers very unique challenges, and we've got to be at our very best to perform there.

“In Brazil, our 2027 recruit Rafa Camara made his debut under extremely challenging conditions and showed us and the world why we signed him for 2027. We're looking forward to building on that for his second race weekend with us.

“Our reserve driver, Ryo Hirakawa, also put in an impressive performance when he was drafted in on Saturday morning in Mexico. He will be back in the car for FP1 in place of Ollie Bearman, now as the 2026 WEC World Champion.

“In recent races, we showed that we can perform at a very high level when everything is working well, and we're looking to get back to performing at the level we showed on Sunday in Mexico.”

title: Behind the lens with Mark Sutton for Antonelli's F1 title triumph
excerpt:
'One of the best experiences of my life' – Mark Sutton on photographing Antonelli's F1 title

From photographing Ayrton Senna to capturing a young Kimi Antonelli meeting Lewis Hamilton, Mark Sutton reflects on four decades documenting Formula 1 and why this season has been one of his most memorable.

Nov 15, 2026 5:06pm UTC

After more than four decades photographing Formula 1's biggest names and most memorable moments, Mark Sutton thought he had seen it all. But Kimi Antonelli's remarkable 2026 season has given the veteran photographer a renewed enthusiasm for his craft.

From capturing a young Antonelli meeting Lewis Hamilton to documenting the Italian's maiden World Championship triumph, Sutton has witnessed some extraordinary moments. Yet it was Antonelli's emotional home victory at Monza that provided one of the highlights of his career.

"That was one of the most incredible experiences of my life," he recalls of Kimi Antonelli's emotional home victory at Monza.

"We posed Kimi up, and there was this sea of people in front of him: 10, 20, 30,000, I don't know how many there were on the circuit.

"It's an experience like nothing else in Formula 1."

It was one of many moments Sutton captured during the Italian's second Formula 1 season, which culminated in a maiden Drivers' Championship in Mexico City and helped Mercedes secure the Constructors' title in Brazil. For Sutton, the experience has also rekindled his enthusiasm for the job.

"All the photographers talk about how amazing he is. It has really kept me going this year because, when you get to 61, the job can become a little repetitive: not boring, but repetitive.

It's great to have a fresh perspective on things and a bit of new life. It's really woken me up. It's been a joy, to be honest, absolutely amazing."

Photographing legends in the making

Sutton's first experience behind a camera at a race came in 1983, when his brother Keith, then working as Ayrton Senna's photographer, invited him to Oulton Park. Sutton was 18, still studying and unfamiliar with the equipment.

"He said, 'I'm going to do the first corner. You go out the back.' I had a camera with no motor drive, so I had to take a picture and then wind the film on manually."

The race featured Senna battling Martin Brundle in British Formula 3, and Sutton suddenly found himself watching a dramatic incident unfold through his lens.

"Senna dived down the inside of Martin Brundle... and the next minute they landed on top of each other. But I didn't get the next frame because I had to wind the film on. By the time I'd done that, it was gone. I did get pictures of them walking around the car afterwards. Those photographs from my first ever race became quite famous."

The photographs became well-known images of Senna's early career, as the Brazilian went on to claim that year's British F3 title before progressing to Formula 1, where he would win three World Championships. Sutton, meanwhile, photographed Senna's first Toleman test and built a career documenting generations of drivers.

"And that was photographing Senna, when nobody really knew what a legend he was going to become," Sutton reflects.

More than three decades later, Sutton would capture another photograph involving a future World Champion, although once again, its significance wouldn't become clear until years afterwards.

At the 2018 Italian Grand Prix, a 12-year-old Antonelli was taking part in the pre-race ceremonies as a grid kid. As the drivers made their way along the line, Sutton was photographing their interactions with the children.

Among those moments was a young Antonelli fist-bumping Lewis Hamilton, then driving for Mercedes.

"My photograph was the one of Kimi with Lewis back in 2018," Sutton reveals.

"Little did I know what that photograph would become. It's crazy, isn't it? Kimi was a grid kid at Monza in 2018. I was photographing the drivers going down the line, high-fiving and fist-bumping the kids. One of those moments was Lewis fist-bumping a 12-year-old Kimi."

Eight years later, the boy in that photograph has succeeded Hamilton at Mercedes and become a World Champion himself.

A sea of Tifosi and a moment in history

Of all the events Sutton photographed in 2026, Antonelli's home victory at Monza stands apart. With thousands of Tifosi flooding the circuit to celebrate their home hero, Sutton found himself on the podium capturing what would become one of the most memorable moments of his career.

"I felt this massive buzz. I turned around afterwards and said to everybody, 'That was one of the best experiences of my life.'

"I think that's what doing this job is about as well, having that chance to experience these things. What other job allows you to travel around the world and take pictures?"

Having attended races with his father since he was just two years old and more than four decades photographing motorsport, Sutton has experienced countless memorable moments, but few atmospheres compare to Monza and the passion of the Italian fans.

"The key thing is the fans. You've got fans in the grandstands, fans on the track, and people down in the pit lane and on the pit wall. It's like a threefold effect. The noise is amazing, and the Italian fans are just incredible."

One image in particular has stayed with him – Antonelli, an Italian flag across his shoulders, standing before the enormous crowd of the Tifosi. Sutton watched as the driver briefly lowered his head, seemingly taking in the scale of the occasion.

Kimi Antonelli of Italy and Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team celebrates on the podium with his trophy during the F1 Grand Prix of Italy at Autodromo Nazionale Monza on September 06, 2026 in Monza, Italy. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Kimi Antonelli with Simone Resta, Deputy Technical Director of Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team during the F1 Grand Prix of Italy at Autodromo Nazionale Monza on September 06, 2026 in Monza, Italy. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Kimi Antonelli on the podium with his trophy during the F1 Grand Prix of Italy at Autodromo Nazionale Monza on September 06, 2026 in Monza, Italy. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Kimi Antonelli drinks Champagne on the podium during the F1 Grand Prix of Italy at Autodromo Nazionale Monza on September 06, 2026 in Monza, Italy. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

"I felt that it was a really important photograph.

"I started shouting to get him to look up. Then he raised his fist and looked directly at me. That was a great picture."

The opportunities continued as Antonelli returned to pose with members of his inner circle.

"I was very lucky because Kimi posed for us, and then he wanted another picture. He came back with his trainer and wanted a picture with him. Then he came back with his engineer, so we carried on taking these photographs."

Sutton later found an elevated position to photograph Mercedes' team celebrations below, while colleagues covered the pit wall, crowd and podium from other angles. Antonelli even removed his shirt and threw it towards the fans, prolonging the celebrations.

"That was probably the most important photo shoot of the season," Sutton says. "I think Getty Images absolutely smashed it. We got every angle possible."

The photographs meant something to the team, too. Weeks later, Mercedes asked Sutton about obtaining the picture of Antonelli with his trainer.

"It's an iconic podium, and it's a privilege to be there photographing somebody who would go on to become World Champion."

Capturing a World Champion in Mexico City

Mexico City brought a different challenge. Antonelli clinched the championship with a podium finish, and Sutton was among the photographers documenting the celebrations that followed.

"The one in Mexico was particularly chaotic. We call it a 'bunfight' because it's literally elbows out," he recalls.

"First, we photographed the team, but his dad and family weren't there, so we had to do it again. Then [Mercedes’ Content Director] Paul Ripke said we'd got all the champagne ready, but there were certain pictures he wanted us to get first.

"All of a sudden, the champagne was handed out and everything went crazy."

The excitement made even an experienced photographer reconsider his position.

"One mechanic lifted Kimi up, but he couldn't see because Kimi was pouring champagne over his face. He was almost walking around blindfolded. It was hilarious. I felt I was too close. I was shooting on a wide lens, a 14-24mm, but I was almost right up his nose. Sometimes you want to be a little farther back."

But Sutton's photographs also captured smaller encounters during the weekend. He watched Antonelli walk along both lines of grid kids, greeting them individually, and photographed a young karter named Emma Garcia Lopez giving him a bracelet, which the Italian was later seen wearing on the podium during his championship celebrations.

"She then shared the story, but she didn't have my photograph, so I completed the story for her with that picture," he explains.

"Knowing that those children in Mexico have interacted with a World Champion is special. It gives them a memento of the race, and maybe a bit of encouragement."

A different side of the champion in Brazil

By the time Formula 1 arrived in Sao Paulo, Antonelli was already champion, while Mercedes would go on to secure the Constructors' Championship. Sutton's most memorable encounters there, however, came away from the racing.

On Thursday, Antonelli surprised him with a fist bump as he arrived at the circuit.

"I'd followed him coming in, and suddenly he put his fist right into my lens," Sutton laughs. "Sometimes you ask drivers to do it, and they will, but with Kimi it felt like a little bit of respect."

The interaction also highlights the mutual appreciation between Antonelli and those documenting his career, something Sutton believes the young champion has understood despite being only in his second F1 season.

"He knows my name. I think generally he'll know all the photographers' names," Sutton says. "He's a clever guy, and he understands that the media is part of this circus and that he has to get them on his side."

Sutton later found himself alone in the pit lane as Antonelli visited the Mercedes mechanics, waved a Brazilian flag and then leaned over to kiss the halo of his car.

"When you're photographing a car on track, you can't really see the driver. You can only see the helmet. Of course, there's a lot of skill involved, and we take some beautiful, amazing photographs. But for me, it's sometimes more about the face: the reactions, the smiles."

He sees echoes of Senna in Antonelli's willingness to joke around with his team, particularly in his playful relationship with race engineer Peter 'Bono' Bonnington. Sutton remembers Senna's prank-filled friendship with Gerhard Berger, although he is careful not to equate the two drivers.

"I think they're different characters, but there are similarities," he says. "I didn't know Senna particularly well, but I think he was quite a joker in the paddock, especially with the teams. I think having that relaxed side is important, rather than being too serious all the time."

A frame of history

Some of Sutton's most significant photographs have taken on new meaning over the years. His early images of Senna and the 2018 photograph of Hamilton meeting a young Antonelli show how moments captured almost by chance can become an important part of Formula 1 history.

"Sometimes that's just how this job works. You're in the right place, with the right lens, the right exposure and the right light."

These fleeting moments, Sutton believes, demonstrate photography's unique ability to preserve the stories and emotions that define the sport.

"I think what it is with photographers is that we capture a particular moment in history. It's frozen. It's not video coverage, where you're filming a particular sequence. We're capturing a sequence as well, but we'll generally use that one particular frame.

"And that one frame can be a magical moment."

Getty Images is now assembling a dedicated collection of Antonelli photographs from the season. Sutton hopes the images will capture not only the trophies and champagne, but also the expressions and interactions that made this championship distinctive.

With three races still remaining, he is looking forward to seeing what else his camera might capture. Yet his memory of Monza is already secure.

"Monza was magical, absolutely magical," he says.

"Kimi has given me a boost, if anything. I'm looking forward to next year now, but I'm also looking forward to the last three races and finishing this season. It's been incredible."

title: Sergio Perez weighs in on Cadillac F1 driver decision ahead of 'crucial' period
excerpt:
Sergio Perez has stated there is not an "easy decision" for Cadillac to make over its driver line-up for the 2027 season.

Perez's position has already been confirmed, having recently signed an extension that will see him through at least the end of 2029.

While Valtteri Bottas was brought into the squad last year on a reported multi-year deal, Cadillac has been pushing for Colton Herta to acquire his super licence, which he successfully did last time out in Mexico City following his latest free practice outing.

Herta is looking to make the jump to F1 despite a disappointing Formula 2 campaign, and Perez insisted that his feedback as a development driver has been valuable.

"Well, I think he's doing a good job," Perez told media including RacingNews365.

"He's bringing good feedback to the team and good information, which is all we need from him.

"Obviously, doing FP1s is always very difficult to show your speed or the level you're at.

"But now I think he's having more time in the car and in the simulator, so we're starting to see more of his speed. Obviously, it's not my decision, but I think it will be down to Marcin to decide who they want in the car.

"I'm also working really well with Valtteri. I think he's been very unfortunate in a few races. There isn't an easy decision for the team."

[Article continues below]

Perez denies role in choosing 2027 team-mate

With Perez committed to the team for the long term, the Mexican is due to play a crucial role in the future of the new squad and aid its development as it seeks to climb the order.

However, the 36-year-old denied that he will assist in the choice of who occupies the second seat for 2027.

"No, not at all. I don't want to, either, because that's not my decision," he said.

"That's why we have someone like Marcin, who will be looking at all the data and information, and he will ultimately make that decision based on what he thinks is best for the future of the team.

"Obviously, we're in a period where we need to evolve extremely quickly. The next three or four months are really crucial in our preparation. So, yeah, I think it's down to him."

title: Liam Lawson handed crushing verdict over delayed Racing Bulls decision
excerpt:
Liam Lawson will continue with Racing Bulls for the 2027 F1 season, after the Faenza-based squad confirmed the New Zealander and Arvid Lindblad last week.

Lawson has been one of the stars of the campaign, whilst his team-mate has enjoyed a strong rookie year in the VCARB 03.

However, Racing Bulls left it late to announce both would stay put, with Red Bull junior and F2 drivers' title hopeful Nikola Tsolov also under consideration.

The Bulgarian will instead focus his efforts on reserve duties for the joint teams and carry out an extensive testing programme, likely in preparation for a full-time seat in 2028.

Although Lindblad was not confirmed either, it is widely accepted that Racing Bulls were weighing up whether to promote Tsolov now and drop Lawson.

That move would have proven unpopular given the 24-year-old's performances this year, which have the Red Bull sister team on the cusp of finishing fifth in the constructors' standings for the first time.

Lawson has scored 89 points and is best of the rest in the drivers' championship after those from the top four teams. That haul is more than Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto's combined 69 points, with their Alpine team sitting sixth in the table.

As such, Lawson was given emphatic backing after Racing Bulls finally confirmed his future, with 95 per cent of fans who voted in a recent poll by RacingNews365 voicing their support for the — albeit delayed — decision.

title: Williams unveil 'chrome' livery tweak for Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
Williams will run a bespoke one-off livery at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, developed alongside title partner Atlassian.

The chrome design features rainbow accents and navy detailing running across the bodywork and engine cover.

The reflective highlights have been placed specifically to catch the light under the floodlit Las Vegas Street Circuit, giving the cars a distinct look when they hit the track on Friday evening.

It's the latest special livery from Williams as it seeks to enjoy a successful weekend at an event it has a history at.

Williams won the inaugural Las Vegas Grand Prix back in 1981 with Alan Jones, and sealed Keke Rosberg's title there the following year.

“We’re proud to be working with Atlassian to unlock that near-50-year history and using it as fuel for our future.

“This spectacular livery reflects that and I’m looking forward to seeing it take to the track under the bright lights of the Vegas Strip.”

title: F1 fans left outraged as disastrous Las Vegas debut sparks $3 million payout - On This Day
excerpt:
On this day three years ago, Formula 1's first practice session for the 2023 Las Vegas Grand Prix was abandoned just minutes after it began, after a loose drain cover tore up the Strip and triggered a chain of events that ended in a lawsuit and a multi-million-dollar settlement.

Carlos Sainz struck the dislodged water valve cover at high speed, destroying his Ferrari's monocoque, internal combustion engine and energy store in one impact.

Esteban Ocon then hit track debris during the red-flag period, cracking his Alpine chassis beyond repair, while Zhou Guanyu suffered serious underside damage that forced Alfa Romeo to build up a replacement tub.

Investigations later confirmed the concrete frame around the fixture had failed under the car's aerodynamic suction.

Race control red-flagged the session after roughly nine minutes and, rather than restart it, called off FP1 entirely as checks were carried out on the rest of the drain covers around the track.

No new start time was ever issued for that session, but FP2 was pushed back to 02:30 local time and extended to 90 minutes to compensate.

That delay meant fans in the grandstands were told to leave around 1:30am, with organisers citing shift limits for security and transport staff. F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali and Las Vegas GP CEO Renee Wilm defended the call in a joint statement.

"We have all been to events, like concerts, games and even other Formula 1 races, that have been canceled because of factors like weather or technical issues," they said. "It happens, and we hope people will understand."

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur was furious at the cost to his team and Sainz was later hit with a 10-place grid penalty for using replacement power unit parts, despite the damage stemming from a circuit defect.

[Article continues below]

Fans take legal action

Organisers initially offered only a $200 merchandise voucher to affected single-day ticket holders, prompting criticism from lawyer Steve Dimopoulos.

"Clearly a $200 merchandise voucher is not a sufficient refund," he said.

Max Verstappen was scathing when told of the compensation offer.

"Then they still make money! Great," Verstappen said. "If I was a fan, I would tear down the whole place. This can't be right."

Dimopoulos Law Firm and JK Legal & Consulting subsequently filed a class action in Nevada on behalf of around 35,000 spectators, alleging breach of contract and deceptive trade practices.

Liberty Media and Las Vegas Grand Prix, Inc. eventually agreed a settlement fund of $3,047,986 for ticket holders, without admitting any wrongdoing.

title: Formula E GEN4 stuns as red flag-fest kickstarts pre-season testing
excerpt:
The opening day of Formula E's 2027 pre-season test is already done and dusted.

Formula E testing kicked off in Madrid on Monday, with seven red flags causing some disruption as Gen4 was officially unleashed.

Despite the volume of red flags, it was an impressive opening day for the Gen4 machinery, with Edoardo Mortara's afternoon lap of 1m 24.344s being a staggering 10 seconds quicker than the Gen3 Evo managed during the Madrid E-Prix earlier this year.

Citroën's Jean-Eric Vergne was fastest during the three-hour morning session, although no 600 kW laps were completed until the afternoon.

Nissan's Zane Maloney was a standout on Day 1, finishing fourth in the morning and second in the afternoon for the Japanese manufacturer.

Morning session

The opening three-hour session of Formula E's 2027 test was a red-flag fest, with the running being halted five times.

The longest stoppage took place after just six minutes following a radio communications issue, causing the session to be suspended for 40 minutes.

Stoppages for Oliver Rowland, Robert Shwartzman and Mitch Evans triggered further interruptions, with the session itself ending under a red flag after Taylor Barnard went off at the first corner.

Two-time champion Jean-Eric Vergne was quickest with a 1m 25.004s, just 0.125s clear of Opel's Mitch Evans.

The top five was completed by the returning Stoffel Vandoorne at Jaguar, Zane Maloney, who is getting accustomed to Nissan, and Pepe Martí.

© 2026 Getty Images

Afternoon session

The afternoon was significantly calmer from a red-flag perspective, with just two being flown across the three hours.

Theo Pourchaire caused the first stoppage 30 minutes into the afternoon after crashing at Turn 3, while Nyck de Vries stopped with just under 25 minutes remaining.

For the first time in Madrid, the afternoon session saw several teams run in full 600 kW mode, with Edoardo Mortara topping the timesheets with a lap time 10 seconds quicker than the Gen3 Evo achieved back in March at Jarama.

Maloney was second and 0.337s adrift of Mortara's 1m 24.344s, while the Porsches found performance to go third and fourth, with Nico Müller ahead of reigning world champion Pascal Wehrlein.

No track action will take place on Tuesday, with Wednesday featuring two more three-hour sessions.

title: Aston Martin unveil major F1 livery change for Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
Aston Martin will run a special one-off livery for this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, created in partnership with CoreWeave.

The revised design marks a departure from the team's usual green identity, with a sweep of white spread across the car replacing much of the familiar paintwork.

Aston Martin said the scheme is intended to visually represent airflow dynamics, tying the car's appearance to the aeromodelling work CoreWeave's cloud infrastructure supports behind the scenes.

Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll will carry the new livery on track for the first time when practice gets underway at the Las Vegas Street Circuit on Thursday night.

“The Las Vegas Grand Prix gives us a fantastic opportunity to showcase the strength of our collaboration with CoreWeave through this unique livery takeover,” said Aston Martin managing director, commerical and marketing.

“What makes this collaboration particularly exciting is the work happening behind the scenes. From helping our engineers make sense of race communications in near real time to identifying new directions in aerodynamic development, we’re seeing how CoreWeave can change the way we operate.

“This is about more than technology for technology’s sake. It’s about giving our people the tools to challenge assumptions, discover new opportunities and keep pushing the boundaries of what’s possible.”

title: Lewis Hamilton seeking £50 million from F1 and FIA as major rule change proposed
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has made a strong appeal to F1 and is asking for increased investment to improve diversity within the paddock.

Lewis Hamilton has called on the FIA and F1 to update their cost cap rules to offer more opportunities to people from disadvantaged backgrounds, while also requesting increased investment from the sport in the coming years.

Hamilton launched 'Mission 44' five years ago with the aim of giving young people from underrepresented backgrounds a greater chance of working in F1.

While the seven-time champion is pleased with the progress he has seen so far, he insisted there is "much still to do" in the release of the latest report.

"Five years ago I asked a simple question about the sport I love: why does it look the way it does?” Hamilton said.

"Not on the podium. In the garages, the design offices, the wind tunnels and the factories. The places where championships are usually won.

"When I walk through the paddock now, I see more women, more Black and Brown faces, more people who look like the fans in the grandstands than at any point since I started.

"That is heartening, and the people behind it deserve credit.

"And yet, there is much still to do. We have opened the door, but we have not yet learned to count how many people walk through it, or how many stay."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

44

Mission 44 suggests change to F1 cost cap

One of the key points from the publication was a call on F1, the FIA and the existing F1 teams to invest £50 million over the next five years.

The report suggested that the “investment can come through any route: F1 teams, F1 and FIA initiatives, and their commercial partners. To count, it should be: additional to 2026 levels of spend; spread across the whole pathway, from aspiration and achievement to access and progression; reported through the common dataset in Recommendation 1, so that it can be tracked to recruitment and retention”.

The scheme was part of one of three main objectives raised in the report, which also suggested that a change should be made to F1's cost cap regulations.

It pointed out that the hiring of new people is hindered because the cost cap counts "apprentice salaries, training and staff development as capped spend", leading to the conclusion that "investment in people competes directly with investment in the car".

Hamilton added: "Here is what I am asking. To every team principal, every chief executive and the leaders of Formula 1 and the FIA: let's make the three recommendations in this report happen.

"Measure who joins, who is promoted and who stays, and let the best practice be recognised.

"Take investment in people out of the cost cap and put money behind the pipeline together. Fix the front door and publish the paid places you will offer every year.

"None of it is beyond a sport that already knows how to measure, improve and be ambitious."

title: Why rapid Red Bull comeback hints at Max Verstappen 2027 title push
excerpt:
Max Verstappen currently sits second in the 2026 drivers' championship, with three races remaining, on 279 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli's commanding 390.

George Russell is third on 262 points, with Lewis Hamilton fourth on 261 and Charles Leclerc fifth on 249, underlining just how competitive the top of the standings has become. But Verstappen's result arrives as something closer to vindication than consolation, given where Red Bull stood just seven months ago.

Back after round five in Canada, Verstappen languished in sixth on just 43 points, ten adrift of Lando Norris in fifth and nowhere near the sharp end of the field, with Antonelli already out front on 131 points.

Red Bull's RB22 had been hampered by an overweight chassis, reportedly running some 12 to 13kg over the 768kg minimum weight limit due to battery packaging demands for the 350kW MGU-K, alongside severe low and medium-speed understeer and tyre degradation problems that had little to do with the power unit itself. T

he car suffered a mechanical and aerodynamic disconnection between its axles, with heavy corner-entry understeer punishing the front tyres before frequently tipping into abrupt oversteer on exit.

The team had also been forced to delay its full pivot to the 2026 regulatory reset while it chased down correlation issues on the previous year's floor, a decision that cost it crucial early development time.

From there, the turnaround has been dramatic. Red Bull restructured its technical department in April, bringing in Ben Waterhouse, previously head of vehicle performance at Sauber and deputy technical director at Toro Rosso, as chief performance and design engineer to work alongside technical director Pierre Wache.

A seven-part upgrade package at the Austrian Grand Prix addressed sidepod inlets and the engine cover to stabilise cooling airflow, along with revised floor surfaces, re-profiled rear suspension fairings, rear corner winglets and a reworked exhaust tailpipe interface.

That was followed by a five-part package introduced in Azerbaijan, covering a reworked floor body, revised diffuser, modified sidepod bodywork, adjusted cooling louvres and reshaped mirror and halo fairings, which proved the real breakthrough, sharpening the car's balance and making it far more predictable to drive.

Gains in straight-line speed followed too, achieved largely through refined energy deployment and software mapping rather than hardware changes, since homologation rules left little room to touch the power unit itself.

Red Bull the best in ICE department

That final detail matters heading into next season. The FIA has identified Red Bull-Ford's engine as the benchmark under its ADUO framework, meaning rivals including Mercedes, Ferrari, Audi and Honda have been handed extra development tokens and budget cap latitude that Red Bull has been denied.

Ferrari, Audi and Honda have reportedly qualified for two additional tokens per season, with Mercedes granted one, alongside financial relief that can run into millions of dollars depending on the measured performance deficit.

With 2027's rule changes shifting the power unit balance further toward the internal combustion engine, trimming rear wing depth by roughly 20mm, and restricting floor fences and plank positioning to cut downforce, Red Bull's chassis gains will be tested against an entirely new baseline.

Verstappen's own future is settled regardless. The four-time champion extended his contract through 2030 in August, having explored options elsewhere earlier in the year before opting to stay, retaining performance-related exit provisions tied to confidential championship thresholds in the process.

Red Bull finished third in the constructors' standings on 415 points, trailing Mercedes' 652 and Ferrari's 510 but ahead of McLaren's 398, a clear marker of how far the Milton Keynes-based outfit dragged itself back into contention after a campaign that once threatened to be forgettable.

title: Toto Wolff reveals surprising Ayrton Senna family stance on Kimi Antonelli
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has opened up on the family of Ayrton Senna warming to Kimi Antonelli as the Italian enjoys a period of success early on in his career.

At the start of November, Antonelli was crowned the youngest driver's champion in F1 history, achieving the title in just his second season.

During his successful campaign in 2026, comparisons were drawn between Senna and Antonelli, but the 20-year-old was quick to shut them down.

Wolff has taken a similar approach, insisting Antonelli is his own style of driver.

“Comparing Kimi to Senna, I mean... I was always not very keen in having this comparison, like Frank [Williams] and Ron [Dennis], Senna is a giant of the sport,” Wolff told media including RacingNews365.

“Who he was as a person, who he was as a racing driver.

“I feel that setting these standards for a 20-year-old driver is a lot of pressure, and that's why I want to not compare him at that stage.

“He's Kimi, Senna was Senna.”

[Article continues below]

Following his title win in Mexico, F1 travelled to Brazil, where Antonelli spent a day with the Senna family.

He continued to honour Senna throughout the race weekend, sporting a helmet design that mirrored the scheme the Brazilian used throughout his own career.

Wolff has stated that the Senna family has warmed to Antonelli, and stated that they see a version of the F1 legend in the young Italian.

“But it's sweet to see how the Senna family embraces him,” he said.

“They say that it's the first time that it looks like there is a second Senninha. That is the first time that you can say, ‘OK, he's a little bit like him’.

“But maybe at that stage he's a Senninha and not a Senna yet. So let the Senninha develop, let him become a Senna.”

title: Lewis Hamilton beats Charles Leclerc but overwhelming Ferrari equal status opinion wins
excerpt:
RacingNews365 readers have delivered a clear verdict on Ferrari's driver policy, with 45 per cent rejecting the idea of a designated number one entirely in favour of drivers settling matters on track.

The poll, which asked whether Ferrari should introduce a clear hierarchy between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, saw Hamilton edge Leclerc among those who do want a pecking order. Forty-one per cent backed the seven-time champion as the man who should be prioritised, compared with 14 per cent for the Monegasque.

Ferrari has run both drivers on equal terms throughout the 2026 campaign, resisting pressure to favour either man despite repeated friction between the two. Team principal Fred Vasseur has defended the approach, arguing that fielding two front-running drivers maximises scoring potential for the team, even while conceding it inevitably creates tension.

That tension boiled over at the Mexico City Grand Prix, when an opening-lap collision between Hamilton and Leclerc cost Ferrari a potential win and triggered fierce internal and media scrutiny. It followed an earlier flashpoint in Shanghai, where contact between the pair while disputing a podium spot prompted questions over whether the pit wall should intervene.

Ferrari's leadership responded by holding mediation talks between Hamilton and Leclerc ahead of the São Paulo Grand Prix, reiterating that team objectives must take precedence over individual battles. Leclerc himself has argued that competing at the front requires two equal, top-level drivers who are always going to clash, making parity preferable to operating with a built-in number two.

In the standings, Hamilton currently sits fourth on 261 points, eight ahead of Leclerc in fifth, with three races remaining. Neither has managed more than a single win this season.

Whether Ferrari introduces formal rules of engagement in the closing rounds remains an open question.

title: Mercedes acquire miracle £1 Formula 1 team after fairytale story
excerpt:
Mercedes-Benz completed its takeover of Brawn GP on this day in 2009, ending one of the most remarkable one-season stories in Formula 1 history.

Daimler AG partnered with Abu Dhabi's Aabar Investments to buy a controlling 75.1 per cent stake in the reigning world champion outfit, with Daimler taking 45.1 per cent and Aabar holding 30 per cent.

Corporate filings later suggested Daimler paid around £77 million for its share, with the full 75.1 per cent package valued at somewhere between £110 million and $170 million, figures that have never been definitively settled across various financial disclosures.

The deal drew a line under a saga that began less than a year earlier. Honda withdrew its works team from Formula 1 in December 2008, citing the financial pressure brought on by the global economic crisis.

Rather than face the enormous redundancy and closure costs of shutting the Brackley factory outright, Honda agreed to a management buyout led by team principal Ross Brawn and chief executive Nick Fry, for a nominal fee of just £1. Honda also left behind an operational budget reported to be around $100 million to help the squad survive its maiden campaign.

That survival turned into domination. The BGP001 carried a double diffuser that exploited a loophole in the floor regulations, feeding a secondary expansion channel through cutouts in the underbody.

Ferrari, Red Bull and Renault protested, but the FIA International Court of Appeal ruled in April 2009 that the design complied fully with the regulations. Brawn's advantage was sharpened further by Honda's early abandonment of in-season development the previous year, which freed up budget and two wind tunnels for the 2009 project.

A fairytale Brawn GP title double

Jenson Button won six of the opening seven races and went on to claim the drivers' championship with 95 points, ahead of Red Bull's Sebastian Vettel on 84 and team-mate Rubens Barrichello on 77. Brawn secured the constructors' title with 172 points, comfortably clear of Red Bull's 153.5.

For Mercedes, the purchase ended years of frustration at McLaren, where Ron Dennis had repeatedly resisted selling a controlling stake. McLaren's move into building its own road cars had also turned it into a direct rival to Mercedes-Benz, making a clean break and full works entry increasingly attractive.

The team has since developed into one of the sport's great modern institutions, now run under a three-way ownership split between Mercedes-Benz Group, Ineos and team principal Toto Wolff, and has grown into one of the most financially valuable operations on the grid.

Since that £1 management buyout, the Brackley squad has amassed 151 race wins and nine constructors' championships under the Mercedes banner.

title: 2027 Formula E pre-season testing - Madrid Day 1 morning results

Citröen's Jean-Eric Vergne topped the opening session of Formula E pre-season testing in Madrid, in what was a session red-flagged five times.

It was a disastrous start to pre-season testing, with a 45-minute red flag having been required after just six minutes following a radio communications problem at the circuit.

Taylor Barnard at Fusion went off in the closing minutes, causing the opening three hours of running to end under the red flag. Nevertheless, it was Vergne quickest on a 1m 25.004.

He was 0.125s clear of Opel's Mitch Evans, with Jaguar's Stoffel Vandoorne, Nissan's Zane Maloney and Cupra Kiro's Pepe Martí completing the top five.
